title: Two perfectly rational players can choose to both lose
body: In the prisoner’s dilemma, two suspects held apart can each stay silent or betray the other. Whatever the partner does, betraying gives each a better personal result, so rational players both betray and both serve longer than if they had both kept quiet. First devised at the RAND Corporation in 1950, the game helps explain price wars, arms races and why climate deals are hard to reach.

slides.heading: The classic payoffs
slides.text: Both stay silent: 1 year each. Both betray: 2 years each. If only one betrays, the betrayer walks free and the silent partner gets 3 years.

slides.heading: Years in prison for you, by what each of you does
slides.note: Whatever your partner does, betraying cuts your own sentence by a year

slides.heading: Play it again
slides.text: In Robert Axelrod’s 1980 computer tournaments of the repeated game, the winner was tit for tat: cooperate first, then copy whatever the other player did last.

slides.heading: The lesson
slides.text: When people expect to meet again, cooperation can pay. That is one reason reputation, repeat customers and long-term contracts matter so much.

slides.question: Which strategy won Axelrod’s repeated-game tournaments?
options: Tit for tat: cooperate, then copy
slides.explanation: Tit for tat cooperates first, then copies whatever the other player did last. When people expect to meet again, cooperation can pay.
